One thing that's really important for them is maintaining balance and harmony in the world. So like most printed people, they believe there are different dimensions and their role is to maintain harmony across these dimensions because that guarantees a happy and prosperous life. The people living today in the forest of Parapane, which is the Amazon, see the entire natural world as saturated with meaning and cosmological significance. Every rock and waterfall embodies a story. Plants and animals are distinct physical manifestations of the same essential spiritual essence.

Every plant and every rock has a life force, and they appreciate the diversity, complexity, and sophistication of different life forces. Even though they can express themselves, they don't have a written language. Their minds are extremely vibrant, dynamic, and energetic. At the same time, more than it appears. The visible world is only one level of perception; behind every tangible form, every plant and animal, is a shadow dimension—a place invisible to ordinary people but visible to shamans. This is the realm of hood spirits, a world of diaphsores where rocks and rivers are alive, plants and animals are human beings, sap and blood are bodily fluids of the primordial river of Anacona, hidden in cataracts behind the physical veil of waterfalls.

In the very center of stones are great moleculus of the hus, where everything is beautiful. The shining feathers, cocoa, calabash of tobacco powdered—its skull and brain of the sun. You can see how the mythology is very complex and how they imbued it into their everyday life. Every day when they wake up and see the world, they see a world of color, energy, and change.

Among the Barasana, such renewal is the fundamental obligation of the living. In practice, this implies that Braz see the earth as potent; the forest is alive with spiritual beings and ancestral powers. To live off the land is to embrace both its creative and destructive potential. Human beings, plants, and animals share the same cosmic origins in a profound sense—they are seen as essentially identical, responsive to the same principles, bound by the same duties, responsible for the collective well-being of creation. There's no separation between nature and culture.

Without the forest and rivers, humans would perish. But without people, the natural world would have no order or meaning; all would be chaos. Thus, the norms that drive social behavior also define the manner in which human beings interact with the wild, plants and animals, multiple phenomena of the natural world—lightning and thunder, the sun and moon, the scent of a blossom, the so sour order of death. Everything is related, everything connected; a single integrated whole.

Mythology infuses land and life with meaning, encoding expectations and behaviors essential to survival in the forest, anchoring each community, each malaka, to a profound spirit of place. One thing that's important because it's a very significant concept is how harmony is seen as a harmonious whole. When you kill something, you first need permission—you need a contract. This is true through most of human history; these people are no different.

When they hunt or fish in the mango forest, it is never trivial. First, a shaman must travel to negotiate with the masters of the animals, forging a mystical contract with the spirit guardians in exchange based on reciprocity. If you kill an animal, you need permission. Now, if you kill the animal, you must thank the animal through ritual sacrifice—compare it to marriage for hunting towards a form of courtship in which one seeks the blessings of a greater authority for the honor of taking into one's family a precious being. Meat is not the right of a hunter but a gift from the spirit world. To kill without permission risks death by the spirit guardian, often in the form of a jaguar, Anacona, tapar, or harpy eagle. The concept here is karma; if you do evil, evil will come to you.
